title: SAMSON DEMANDED A PHILISTINE WOMAN—EVEN AFTER HIS PARENTS QUESTIONED THE MARRIAGE
paragraphs: SAMSON DEMANDED A PHILISTINE WOMAN—EVEN AFTER HIS PARENTS QUESTIONED THE MARRIAGE
He saw what he wanted. His parents saw the danger. God saw a battlefield. And buried inside Samson’s scandal is a warning for every believer who has ever confused desire with destiny.
There are moments in Scripture that make you uncomfortable because the people God uses do not behave the way you expect people used by God to behave.
Samson is one of those people.
Before Delilah.
Before the haircut.
Before the blinded warrior stood between the pillars of a Philistine temple.
Before the name Samson became synonymous with extraordinary strength and catastrophic weakness...
there was a woman.
And one sentence.
A sentence that should make every believer who has ever desperately wanted something stop and examine the heart.
Samson went down to Timnah.
He saw a Philistine woman.
Then he went home and essentially told his parents:
Get her for me.
I want her as my wife.
His parents questioned him.
Samson insisted.
And then Scripture says something so startling that, if we read it carelessly, we can completely misunderstand both Samson and God.
Because Judges 14:4 tells us that something in this unfolding confrontation was “from the LORD.”
Wait.
What?
Did God approve Samson’s every desire?
Was Samson’s attraction automatically holy because God would ultimately use the situation?
Does the fact that God can accomplish His purposes through a broken decision mean the brokenness suddenly becomes righteousness?
No.
And this is where Samson’s story stops being an ancient story about a strong man with terrible relationship problems...
and starts walking uncomfortably close to your own front door.
Samson’s story did not begin with a woman.
It began with God.

Israel had again fallen into evil, and the Philistines oppressed them for forty years. Into that darkness, the angel of the LORD announced the birth of a child who would be specially consecrated to God.
Judges 13 says Samson would be a Nazirite to God from the womb and would “begin to deliver Israel” from Philistine domination.
Think about that.
Before Samson could walk, there was calling.
Before Samson could choose anything, there was consecration.
Before Samson ever saw the woman in Timnah, God had already declared that his life belonged to a purpose greater than his appetites.
That makes what happens next so painful.
Judges 14 opens almost abruptly:
Samson goes down to Timnah.
He sees a Philistine woman.
He returns to his parents.
And he wants her.
The Hebrew makes his insistence particularly revealing.
When his parents object, Samson says:
אוֹתָהּ קַח־לִי כִּי־הִיא יָשְׁרָה בְעֵינָי
’Otah qach-li, ki-hi yashrah be‘enai.
The sense is:
“Get her for me, because she is right in my eyes.”
Or, idiomatically, “She is right for me.”
That expression should make readers of Judges uneasy.
בְּעֵינַי — be‘enai
“In my eyes.”
Samson saw something.
Samson wanted something.
And what he saw looked right to him.
That sounds frighteningly familiar.
Because some of the most dangerous words a human heart can whisper are:
“But it feels right to me.”
I know what Scripture says...
but this feels right.
I know people who love me are warning me...
but this feels right.
I know I am becoming spiritually colder...
but this feels right.
I know I have started hiding things...
but this feels right.
I know I cannot pray about this with the same honesty anymore...
but surely God understands.
Samson’s parents saw a problem their son did not appear interested in seeing.
They asked why he needed to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines rather than from among his own people. Judges 14 explicitly records their objection and Samson’s continued insistence.
But then comes the sentence that changes the entire scene.
וְאָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ לֹא יָדְעוּ כִּי מֵיְהוָה הִיא
Ve’aviv ve’immo lo yade‘u ki meYHWH hi...
His father and mother did not know that this was “from the LORD.”
The verse continues by explaining that an occasion was being sought against the Philistines, who were ruling over Israel.
This is one of those verses where humility matters.
We should not make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
The text does not give us permission to transform Samson’s impulses into a model of godly romantic discernment.
Rather, it reveals something far greater about the sovereignty of God:
God was capable of using this explosive situation in His larger purpose against Israel’s oppressors.
That distinction matters enormously.
God using something does not necessarily mean God morally endorses everything human beings did within it.
God is sovereign enough to accomplish His purposes even through tangled motives, human weakness, disastrous consequences, hostile enemies, and situations that seem completely out of control.
That is not permission to sin.
It is a reason to worship.
Because if God could work through Samson’s complicated story, your failures have not somehow become stronger than His sovereignty.
But do not twist grace into permission.
There is a dangerous counterfeit gospel that whispers:
“God can use my mistakes, so my choices do not really matter.”
Samson’s life destroys that lie.
Yes, God used Samson.
And Samson suffered terribly.
Those two realities stand beside each other.

The Spirit of the LORD empowered Samson with extraordinary strength. Judges records the Spirit coming powerfully upon him repeatedly. Yet the narrative also exposes a man whose appetites and impulses repeatedly brought devastation into his life.
Calling did not make him consequence-proof.
Giftedness did not make him spiritually invincible.
Strength did not make him wise.
And being used by God did not mean every choice he made pleased God.
Someone reading this needs that sentence.
Because perhaps people admire your ministry.
Your talent.
Your intelligence.
Your generosity.
Your Bible knowledge.
Your ability to encourage everyone else.
Perhaps people see strength when they look at you.
But there is something you keep allowing because it looks right in your own eyes.
Nobody sees it.
Yet.
Maybe it is a relationship you know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
Maybe it is pornography you promised would be “just one more time.”
Maybe it is resentment you have learned to disguise as discernment.
Maybe it is secret flirting you insist is harmless.
Maybe it is money becoming your real security.
Maybe it is pride hiding underneath ministry.
Maybe it is bitterness.
Maybe it is an addiction.
Maybe you keep asking God to bless something you have never genuinely surrendered to Him.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that your life still appears strong.
Samson was strong too.
That is the warning.
You can possess remarkable gifts while carrying dangerous weaknesses.
You can experience God’s mercy while still needing repentance.
You can know Scripture and still rationalize desire.
You can look powerful publicly while becoming vulnerable privately.
And sometimes the enemy does not need to destroy your strength.
He only needs to convince you that because you are strong in one area, you cannot fall in another.
Samson could tear apart a lion.
But physical strength could not automatically govern his heart.
Imagine that.

A lion comes roaring toward him near the vineyards of Timnah, and the Spirit of the LORD comes powerfully upon Samson. With no weapon in his hands, Samson tears the animal apart. Judges 14 records the extraordinary event plainly.
He could defeat what terrified ordinary men.
Yet the greater battle was always closer.
Inside.
That is where many of us lose.
We are fighting demons “out there” while refusing to confront desires “in here.”
We rebuke darkness but excuse pride.
We quote Scripture publicly and negotiate with temptation privately.
We want victory over circumstances while resisting Christ’s lordship over our appetites.
We want Samson’s strength without Samson’s warning.
But Scripture loves us too much to give us sanitized heroes.
The Bible does not airbrush Samson.
It does not hide Abraham’s fear.
It does not hide Jacob’s deception.
It does not hide David’s adultery.
It does not hide Peter’s denial.
And it does not hide Samson’s appetite.
Why?
Because the Bible is ultimately not the story of impressive human beings rescuing themselves.
It is the story of a holy and faithful God working through a fallen world while moving history toward the One Savior who does not fail.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where Samson’s story becomes even more powerful.
Samson was a deliverer.
But Samson needed deliverance.
Jesus is different.
Samson was announced before birth as one who would begin Israel’s deliverance from the Philistines.
Jesus came to accomplish the deeper rescue humanity could never accomplish for itself.
Samson’s enemies bound him.
Jesus willingly submitted Himself to arrest.
Samson’s story became entangled with personal vengeance.
Jesus prayed for His executioners.
Samson ultimately died while destroying enemies.
Jesus died to save His enemies.
Samson’s death brought judgment upon Philistine oppressors.
Christ’s death bore judgment for sinners who trust in Him.
Samson stretched out his arms between pillars and died.
Centuries later, outside Jerusalem, Jesus Christ stretched out His arms upon a cross.
But Jesus was not another flawed judge.
He was the sinless Son of God.
The Lamb of God.
The true Savior.
Samson could begin a temporary deliverance.
Jesus could cry:
“It is finished.”
And that is why your scandal does not have to be your final chapter.
Maybe you have made choices because they were right in your own eyes.
Maybe your parents warned you.
Maybe your pastor warned you.
Maybe your spouse pleaded with you.
Maybe Scripture convicted you.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has been pressing the same wound for months.
And you kept saying:
I know.
But I want it.
Perhaps you got what you wanted.
And now you are living with what wanting it cost.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin did not matter.
The Gospel says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion is harmless.
Grace is God offering guilty sinners forgiveness purchased by the blood of His Son.
That means you do not need another excuse.
You need Jesus.
You do not need to convince yourself that everything was “meant to happen.”
You need repentance.
You do not need to rewrite your past until your sin looks innocent.
Bring the truth into the light.
Call sin what God calls it.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
Because one of the most beautiful truths in all Scripture is that God does extraordinary things with people whose stories contain chapters they wish they could erase.
Not because scandal becomes righteousness.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because grace is greater than the finality we assign to our failures.
Even Samson’s story did not end in Judges 14.
There would be anger.
Violence.
Loss.
More compromise.
Delilah.
Betrayal.
Chains.
Blindness.
Humiliation.
A man once feared for supernatural strength would eventually be led around by others.
And yet...
even there...
Samson prayed.
At the end of his ruined strength, Samson turned again toward the God who had never ceased to be God.
And centuries later, Hebrews 11 would actually include Samson among people remembered in connection with faith.
What astonishing mercy.
Not a perfect man.
Not an uncomplicated story.
Not a spotless record.
A broken man whose name still appears in the biblical testimony of faith.
That is not permission to imitate Samson’s sins.
It is permission to stop believing that failure places you beyond the reach of God’s mercy.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Not because you need to hear that Samson was strong.
You already know that.
Maybe you needed to discover that the strongest man in the room could still desperately need grace.
And so can you.
Maybe your marriage is hurting.
Maybe your children barely recognize the person you have become.
Maybe lust has eaten years of your spiritual life.
Maybe you compromised.
Maybe you returned to the thing Christ delivered you from.
Maybe you feel like a hypocrite walking into church.
Maybe everybody thinks you are doing well while you are exhausted from maintaining the appearance.
Then stop performing.
Come home.
Jesus already knows the chapter you are hiding.
He saw the decision.
He saw the message.
He saw the browser history.
He heard the lie.
He knows the resentment.
He knows why you did it.
He knows what happened afterward.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up enough so Christ might tolerate you.”
It is:
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing.
There is mercy.
There is restoration.
There is a new way to live.
And there is something Samson desperately teaches us:
Do not wait until the pillars are around you to surrender what God is confronting today.
Do not wait until desire becomes bondage.
Do not wait until compromise becomes identity.
Do not wait until secrecy becomes captivity.
Do not wait until you lose something precious before deciding that obedience was precious all along.
Ask yourself the question Samson’s story forces upon us:
What looks right in my eyes right now that I have never honestly placed before the eyes of God?
Stay there for a moment.
What is it?
A person?
A relationship?
A habit?
A secret?
An ambition?
An offense you refuse to forgive?
Something you desperately want God to approve?
You do not have to tell the entire internet what happened.
But you should stop lying to God about it.
Not as a performance.
As a confession.
Let other believers stand with you.
Someone reading silently may need evidence that repentance is not the end of a person’s story.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who looks strong but is quietly losing a battle nobody knows exists.
Not for numbers.
Not for applause.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday’s conviction difficult to remember tomorrow.
Come back when something begins looking “right in your eyes” and ask again whether it is right before God.
Supporting Gospel work can be a genuine way to glorify God when it is done freely, gratefully, wisely, and for the advance of Christ-centered ministry.
It is discipleship.
It is helping truth keep moving.
It is standing behind a mission that wants to put Christ before another exhausted believer at two in the morning...
another marriage hanging by a thread...
another person hiding an addiction...
another Christian drifting into compromise...
another skeptic wondering whether grace could possibly be real...
another Samson who still thinks strength means he cannot fall.

One shared article cannot save anyone—Jesus saves—but God can use a shared truth, a Scripture passage, a testimony, or a faithful invitation to put the Gospel in front of someone at the moment they desperately need to hear it.
Samson wanted what looked right in his own eyes.
His story reminds us how dangerous that can become.
But Samson's failures were never bigger than God's sovereignty.
And your worst chapter is not greater than the grace offered to you in Jesus Christ.
So repent while your heart can still hear the warning.
Return while grace is calling.
Stop defending what Christ is asking you to surrender.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy is not discovering that something you wanted was wrong.
Perhaps it is discovering it was wrong...
and still refusing to let it go.
You may have written a chapter in your life that you would give anything to erase—but at the cross, Jesus proves that your darkest chapter does not have to write your final sentence.
